extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of literature, drama, and classical criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying Aristotle's evaluative criteria for poetry, tragedy, and comedy (plot, character, diction, music, spectacle, metre, unity, etc.) as presented in the Poetics with commentary. Useful for analyzing or composing dramatic/epic/lyric works in a classical-critical frame.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: A Tragedy is the portrayal of an imaginary chapter of heroic life, complete and of some length, in language sweetened in different parts in all known ways, in dramatic, not narrative form, indirectly through pity and terror (producing catharsis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasises dramatic (not narrative) presentation, an imaginary but complete episode of a hero's life, and the elicitation of pity and terror culminating in katharsis. 'Sweetened language' refers to rhythm, mixture with the unfamiliar (harmony), and tune; only certain parts are restrained by metre or tune. The dramatis personae must be conscious and responsible beings whose conduct arises from character and intellect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Six Factors of Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: A Tragedy must thus have six Factors, analytically speaking: Story, Psychology (Character), Diction, Intelligence (Thought/Reasoning), Presentation, Music.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two factors (Diction, Music) are Clothing, one (Treatment) corresponds to Presentation or mode, and three (Story, Psychology, Intelligence) go to the Theme. These are the exhaustive analytical components for evaluating or composing Tragedy; each factor should be considered for its contribution to the whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot / Story (unity and completeness)
rubrics_metrics.description: The fictitious chapter of life is the Story: a group of occurrences forming a complete episode (unity of theme) suitable for dramatic treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plot should be a complete and coherent sequence of incidents (a beginning, middle, end) producing a unified action. Aristotle privileges 'unity of theme' (unity of action); Tragedy traditionally aims to keep within, or nearly within, a revolution of the sun (unity of time) to preserve time-illusion and continuity. The critic should judge how well the eide (forms) of plot realize this unity and completeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character / Psychology
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters must be conscious and responsible beings whose specific qualities derive from character and intellect; these traits determine fictitious conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Character consistency and plausibility are essential: actions should flow from established traits. The text notes examples (Micawber, Skimpole) to show how abstraction of a trait yields comic types; in tragedy, characters must be suitable for generating pity and terror without violating their nature. Defects used for comic effect must not 'destroy the nature' of the thing in which they occur (i.e., not cause real pain or destruction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Intelligence / Thought / Reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Passages in which characters demonstrate propositions or formulate opinions — the play's reasoning or intellectual content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thought (intelligence) governs the persuasive and reflective moments of a drama: speeches that reveal character, motive, and argumentative structure. Evaluate the clarity, appropriateness and dramatic integration of such moments; reasoning should serve the plot and contribute to eliciting pity/terror (in tragedy) or to the comedic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction / Language (including 'sweetening')
rubrics_metrics.description: By language Aristotle means the material of versification; 'sweetened' language includes rhythm, mixture with the unfamiliar (harmony), and tune.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diction is judged for clarity, appropriateness, and aesthetic effect. Sweetenings (rhythm/period, mixture of the familiar with the foreign, and tune) tickle the ear and help take the hearer out of the real world. Only certain parts of the drama are restrained by metre or tune; diction must balance the familiar (for understanding) with the unfamiliar (for aesthetic elevation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Music / Melody
rubrics_metrics.description: Musical composition is a factor whose whole force is on the surface; music is a direct, universal language distinct from verbal poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the contribution of music to the drama's emotional effect — its directness, its fit to the action, and how it 'sweetens' parts of the drama. Music differs from verbal poetry in immediacy; it supports rhythm and mood and helps produce the audience's affective response (katharsis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation / Spectacle (including chorus, masks, actors, scenery)
rubrics_metrics.description: Presentation is a necessary factor: the dramatis personae go through their parts themselves; presentation includes acting, staging, chorus, masks, and scenic apparatus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the effectiveness of physical and performative elements (acting, choreography, masks, chorus behaviour, scene-painting). Historical notes: number of actors increased (one → two by Aeschylus; a third actor with scenery by Sophocles); masks render actors ridiculous in comedy; chorus and puppet-show elements reflect origin and function. Presentation can shift emphasis (e.g., Aeschylus concentrated interest on discourse at expense of dance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of Time (length constraint)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy traditionally tries to keep within, or nearly within, a revolution of the sun (i.e., a single day's action).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The unity of time enhances time-illusion and dramatic plausibility; longer periods strain scenic and technical resources and dilute the immediacy of action. Critics should judge whether temporal compression/continuity serves the unity of action and the audience's perception of inevitability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meter selection and appropriateness
rubrics_metrics.description: Different metres suit different functions: iambic resembles conversational rhythm (suitable for dialogue and many tragic passages), trochee aligns with primitive dances, hexameter suits epic, anapaest has an 'attack' effect; metres are often tied to social function or labour-rhythms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose metre to match content and performative origin: iambic for conversational or invective uses; hexameter for epic narrative; trochaic for dance-dominated pieces. The commentary gives ethnographic and functional analogies (Boucher assigns metres to types of labour; anapaest as assault rhythm). Meter also aids memory and oral transmission; consider its mnemonic and affective roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy: definition and limits for the ludicrous
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy is the portrayal of an inferior class, yet not in all their inferiority — the ludicrous side of ugliness abstracted. Ludicrousness is of the genus 'failing'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'failing' that produces laughter must be painless and non-destructive; it must not 'destroy the nature' of what it affects (so that the audience remains amused rather than pained). Common comic devices include depiction of vices (e.g., drunkenness) that cause neither pain nor catastrophe. Cultural sensitivity: what is amusing to some may be painful to others (e.g., mockery of disability). Evaluate whether the comic treatment abstracts ludicrousness appropriately without cruelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wit, ambiguity, and intelligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Ambiguity can be witty when it arouses a harmless double-meaning or 'does not hurt nor harm'; it is not witty when it leads to serious misunderstanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Witticisms should preserve clarity of communication; a play may employ ambiguity for comic or rhetorical effect provided it does not cause harmful confusion. Example: a poet refusing to write about the king because 'the king was no subject' — witty ambiguity that avoids misunderstanding. Assess whether linguistic playfulness enhances effect without undermining comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of origin-elements (dance, ritual, and magical function)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry and drama grew from music, dance, ritual, and sometimes magic (e.g., invective metre, phallic rites, sympathetic-magic origins); these origins influence suitable form and content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing or evaluating, consider the performative roots: certain dances or rituals supply rhythms, choruses, obscene or religious elements, and masks. The critic should be aware that some features (choral forms, obscene remnants, ritual timing) are historically conditioned and may inform genre expectations and audience response.
